formulas.name: Slack Time
formulas.vars: LS: latest a task can start without delaying project · ES: earliest a task can start
formulas.when: Calculating flexibility in a project schedule. A task on the critical path has zero slack.
formulas.ex: Task A can start on Day 3 (ES) but must start by Day 5 (LS) to not delay the project. Slack = 5 - 3 = 2 days. ✓

formulas.name: Triple Constraint Relationship
formulas.vars: Scope: project deliverables & quality · Time: schedule · Resources: budget & staff
formulas.when: Evaluating the impact of any project change. You cannot change one without impacting at least one other.
formulas.trap: Adding scope without increasing time or resources is a primary cause of project failure.

formulas.name: Data Storage Conversion
formulas.vars: TB: Terabyte · GB: Gigabyte · MB: Megabyte · KB: Kilobyte
formulas.when: Calculating storage needs or understanding data volume.
formulas.ex: A 2 TB hard drive has 2 * 1024 = 2048 GB of space. ✓

formulas.name: Conversion Rate
formulas.vars: Conversions: desired actions (e.g., purchases, sign-ups) · Visitors: total users on site
formulas.when: Measuring the effectiveness of a website or marketing campaign.

formulas.name: ★ SQL SELECT with Implicit Join
formulas.formula: SELECT t1.col, t2.col FROM table1 t1, table2 t2 WHERE t1.key = t2.key AND [conditions];
formulas.vars: t1, t2 are table aliases · col is a column name · key is the joining field
formulas.when: Querying data from two related tables in a relational database.
formulas.trap: Omitting the `WHERE t1.key = t2.key` join condition is WRONG and will produce a Cartesian product (all possible row combinations).
formulas.ex: SELECT P.Part_Name, S.Supplier_Name FROM PART P, SUPPLIER S WHERE P.Supplier_Number = S.Supplier_Number AND P.Part_Number = 137; → Door latch, CBM Inc. ✓

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with Explicit JOIN
formulas.formula: SELECT t1.col, t2.col FROM table1 t1 JOIN table2 t2 ON t1.key = t2.key WHERE [conditions];
formulas.vars: JOIN specifies the tables to link · ON specifies the join condition
formulas.when: Using modern, more readable SQL syntax for joining tables. Functionally equivalent to the implicit join.
formulas.ex: SELECT P.Part_Name, S.Supplier_Name FROM PART P JOIN SUPPLIER S ON P.Supplier_Number = S.Supplier_Number WHERE P.Part_Number = 137; → Door latch, CBM Inc. ✓

formulas.name: Early Start Time (ES)
formulas.formula: ES = Max(EF of all immediate predecessors)
formulas.vars: EF is the Early Finish time of a preceding task.
formulas.when: Calculating the earliest possible moment a task can begin in a project schedule (Critical Path Method).
formulas.ex: Task A (EF=Day 3) and Task B (EF=Day 5) are predecessors to Task C. ES for Task C = Max(3, 5) = Day 5. ✓

formulas.name: Late Start Time (LS)
formulas.vars: LF is the Late Finish time · Duration is the task's length.
formulas.when: Calculating the latest possible moment a task can begin without delaying the project's end date.
formulas.ex: A task has a duration of 3 days and a Late Finish of Day 10. Its Late Start = 10 - 3 = Day 7. ✓

formulas.name: Kilobyte (KB) Conversion
formulas.vars: A byte is 8 bits, representing one character.
formulas.when: Converting between units of digital storage.
formulas.ex: A 5 KB text file is 5 * 1,024 = 5,120 bytes. ✓

formulas.name: Megabyte (MB) Conversion
formulas.vars: MB is a common unit for file sizes like photos and songs.
formulas.when: Converting between units of digital storage.

formulas.name: Gigabyte (GB) Conversion
formulas.vars: GB is a common unit for storage device capacity (e.g., phone storage, SSDs).
formulas.when: Converting between units of digital storage.
formulas.ex: A 16 GB USB drive holds 16 * 1,024 = 16,384 MB. ✓

formulas.name: Terabyte (TB) Conversion
formulas.vars: TB is a common unit for large hard drives and data archives.
formulas.when: Converting between units of digital storage.
formulas.ex: A 2 TB hard drive holds 2 * 1,024 = 2,048 GB. ✓

formulas.name: ★ Petabyte (PB) Conversion
formulas.vars: PB Petabyte · TB Terabyte
formulas.when: Converting between large-scale data storage units.
formulas.ex: A data warehouse with 2,048 TB of data has 2 PB. ✓

formulas.name: ★ Exabyte (EB) Conversion
formulas.vars: EB Exabyte · PB Petabyte
formulas.when: Converting between very large-scale (Big Data) storage units.
formulas.ex: A global social media platform stores 3 EB of photo data, which is 3,072 PB. ✓

formulas.name: Estimate to Complete (ETC)
formulas.formula: ETC = (Budget at Completion - Earned Value) / Cost Performance Index
formulas.vars: A forecast of how much more the project will cost to finish.
formulas.when: Used in Earned Value Management to forecast future project costs.

formulas.name: Estimate at Completion (EAC)
formulas.formula: EAC = Actual Cost + Estimate to Complete
formulas.vars: A forecast of the total cost of the project at its end.
formulas.when: Used in Earned Value Management to see if the project will finish over or under budget.

formulas.name: SQL ORDER BY Clause
formulas.formula: SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name ORDER BY column1 [ASC|DESC];
formulas.vars: ASC ascending (default) · DESC descending
formulas.when: Sorting the result set of a query.
formulas.ex: SELECT Part_Name, Unit_Price FROM PART ORDER BY Unit_Price DESC; → returns parts from most to least expensive. ✓

formulas.name: SQL WHERE with AND/OR
formulas.formula: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE condition1 AND (condition2 OR condition3);
formulas.vars: AND requires all conditions to be true · OR requires at least one condition to be true · () enforce precedence
formulas.when: Filtering records based on multiple criteria.
formulas.trap: Forgetting parentheses with OR is WRONG because AND has higher precedence, leading to unexpected results.
formulas.ex: WHERE Part_Number = 137 OR Part_Number = 150; → returns two specific parts. ✓

formulas.name: Zettabyte (ZB) Conversion
formulas.vars: ZB Zettabyte · EB Exabyte
formulas.when: Converting at the highest scale of data storage, relevant for global internet traffic.

formulas.name: SQL GROUP BY Clause
formulas.formula: SELECT column_name, AGG_FUNC(column_name) FROM table_name GROUP BY column_name;
formulas.vars: AGG_FUNC an aggregate function like SUM(), COUNT(), AVG()
formulas.when: Grouping rows that have the same values into summary rows.
formulas.ex: SELECT Supplier_Number, COUNT(*) FROM PART GROUP BY Supplier_Number; → shows how many parts each supplier provides. ✓

concepts.def: The measure of the number of links or relationships between two data entities. It defines how tables are related.
The sequence of tasks in a project that determines the total length of the project. Any delay in a critical path task delays the entire project.
A three-step process to load data into a data warehouse. Extract: obtain data from sources. Transform: cleanse and normalize the data. Load: organize and catalog the data in the warehouse.
A computing model where significant processing is performed on a central server, and the client device is mainly for input and display. This is a server-centric architecture.
Analog signals are continuous physical waves (like sound). Digital signals are discrete, using binary numbers (0s and 1s) to represent information.
A type of surveillance technology used to monitor and record each keystroke typed on a specific computer's keyboard. Can be software or a physical hardware device (e.g., USB 'Rubber Ducky').
The process of identifying, assessing, and controlling threats to an organization's capital and earnings. In projects, it involves determining high-risk areas and developing plans to mitigate them.

The process of creating, sharing, using, and managing the knowledge and information of an organization. It refers to a multidisciplinary approach to achieving organizational objectives by making the best use of knowledge.
A group of people who share a concern or a passion for something they do and learn how to do it better as they interact regularly.
The percentage of users who take a desired action. The archetypal example is the percentage of website visitors who buy something on the site.
The practice of obtaining information or input into a task or project by enlisting the services of a large number of people, either paid or unpaid, typically via the Internet.
The practice and science of classification of things or concepts, including the principles that underlie such classification.
A Primary Key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A Foreign Key is a primary key from one table that is used in a second table to form a link between them.
The process of streamlining complex data structures to minimize redundant data and awkward relationships. This improves data integrity.
Data are raw, unorganized facts. Information is data that has been processed, organized, and structured into a meaningful form.

A Data Warehouse is a large, centralized repository of data from many sources across an enterprise. A Data Mart is a smaller, focused subset of a data warehouse that deals with a single subject or line of business.
A tool that enables users to quickly analyze multidimensional data from multiple perspectives. It's used for business intelligence and is insulated from operational processing.

A strategic management performance metric that helps companies identify and improve various internal functions and their resulting external outcomes. It measures performance on four dimensions: Financial, Customer, Business Process, and Learning & Growth.
The three key constraints of project management: Scope, Time, and Resources (Cost). A change in one constraint necessitates a change in at least one of the others to maintain balance.
A type of bar chart that illustrates a project schedule. It lists tasks to be performed on the vertical axis and time intervals on the horizontal axis, showing start/end dates and dependencies.
A method of grouping data into packets that are transmitted over a digital network. Packets can take different paths and are reassembled at the destination.
Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol. The fundamental suite of communication protocols used to interconnect network devices on the internet. It governs how data is transmitted.
The internet's phonebook. It converts human-readable domain names (like www.google.com) into machine-readable IP addresses (like 172.217.14.228).
Creates a secure, encrypted connection over a less secure network, such as the public internet. It encrypts messages to protect them from snooping.

A technology that uses radio waves to read and capture information stored on a tag attached to an object. A tag can be read from up to several feet away and does not need to be within direct line-of-sight of the reader.
In Tableau, Dimensions are qualitative (categorical) data that set the level of detail (e.g., Category, Region). Measures are quantitative numerical data that can be aggregated (e.g., Sales, Profit).
In Tableau, a Join combines tables of data on a row-by-row basis from the same data source. A Blend links data from multiple, separate data sources at an aggregate level.

A Dashboard is a collection of related views and objects arranged to communicate a data story, often interactively. A Story is a sequence of visualizations that work together to convey information, like a presentation.
The international standard language for processing a database. Used to read, insert, modify, and delete data.
Massive sets of unstructured or semi-structured data from sources like web traffic, social media, and sensors. Volumes are too large for typical DBMS.

A distributed computing model where tasks are partitioned between providers of a resource or service, called servers, and service requesters, called clients. The exam answer 'server concentric' likely refers to this model. Example: A web browser (client) requests a webpage from a web server.

A type of hardware keylogger that masquerades as a generic USB device. It injects pre-programmed keystroke payloads into a machine, often used to install malware or exfiltrate data. Example: An attacker plugs a Rubber Ducky into an unlocked computer, which then automatically opens a command prompt and downloads a malicious file.

Two methods for delivering BI results. Push Publishing delivers BI to users without a request, on a schedule or triggered by an event. Pull Publishing requires the user to request BI results. Example: A sales manager receives a 'Push' sales report every Monday morning via email. An analyst uses 'Pull' to run an ad-hoc query on a dashboard.

The structured organization of data in a database, from the smallest to the largest unit. The hierarchy is: Byte (a single character) -> Field/Column -> Record/Row -> Table/File -> Database. Example: The character 'J' is a byte in the 'FirstName' field of a record for 'John Smith' in the 'Customers' table.

A set of rules that a relational database management system (RDBMS) uses to ensure that relationships between tables remain consistent. It prevents users from entering inconsistent data. Example: If a `CustomerID` in the `Orders` table must exist in the `Customers` table, referential integrity prevents you from adding an order for a non-existent customer.

Core components of a dimensional model in a data warehouse. A Fact Table contains quantitative measures of a business process (the 'facts'). A Dimension Table contains descriptive attributes that provide context to the facts. Example: A `Sales` fact table contains `UnitsSold` and `Revenue`. A `Product` dimension table contains `ProductName` and `Category`.

Specialized software that is stored in non-volatile, read-only memory on a hardware device. It provides low-level control for the device's specific hardware. Example: The BIOS or UEFI on a computer's motherboard that runs when you first turn it on is firmware.

A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to be carried out by a project team to accomplish the project objectives and create the required deliverables. Example: A WBS for building a house would have top-level items like 'Foundation', 'Framing', and 'Electrical', each broken down into smaller tasks.

Two ways Tableau can connect to a data source. A 'Live' connection sends queries directly to the source database, providing real-time data. An 'Extract' connection takes a snapshot of the data and loads it into Tableau's high-performance in-memory data engine. Example: Use a Live connection for a real-time sales dashboard. Use an Extract for a large, static dataset to improve performance.

In Tableau, fields can be discrete or continuous. Discrete fields (blue pills) have individually separate and distinct values, used to create headers. Continuous fields (green pills) have values that form an unbroken whole, used to create axes. Example: 'Region' (East, West) is discrete. 'Sales' ($100, $101.50) is continuous.

Visually represents data by comparing a value across different categories. The length of the bar is the primary means of visual comparison. Example: Comparing sales figures for different product categories.
Connects related data points (marks) to show movement or a relationship over time or another continuous variable. Example: Tracking monthly sales revenue over a year.

The process of managing all activities for the adoption and routinization of an innovation or new system. It is required for successful system building to counter user resistance. Example: A series of training workshops and regular email updates before a new software rollout.

Unstructured decisions made by upper management that define the organization’s overall goals and future direction. They answer the 'WHY?' questions. Example: Deciding whether to expand into a new international market.

A person, place, thing, or event on which we store and maintain information. In a database, an entity is typically represented by a table. Example: In a university database, 'Student', 'Professor', and 'Course' are all entities.

A network that connects computers and devices in a limited geographical area such as a home, school, or office building. Example: The Wi-Fi network in your house connecting your laptop, phone, and printer.

A network that spans a large geographical area, such as a state, province, or country. The Internet is the world's largest WAN. Example: A corporation's network connecting its offices in New York, London, and Tokyo.
Uses past performance data to predict future trends and behaviors. Example: Using a customer's purchasing history to predict which future products they are likely to buy.

Uses analysis of current data and situations to recommend one or more courses of action (optimization, simulation). Example: A GPS application calculating the fastest route based on current traffic conditions.

A characteristic or quality describing an entity. In a database table, attributes are the columns or fields. Example: For the 'Student' entity, attributes would be 'Student_ID', 'FirstName', and 'Major'.
A unique 32-bit number assigned to every device connected to the Internet, used to identify and locate it on the network. Example: 207.46.250.119.

Volatile memory requires power to maintain the stored information; its contents are lost when power is turned off. Non-volatile memory retains its data even when power is off. Example: Volatile is RAM; Non-volatile is an SSD or hard disk drive (HDD).

An 'Intelligent Technique' that captures the tacit knowledge of a human expert as a set of rules in a software system. It uses a knowledge base and an inference engine to solve problems. Example: A medical diagnosis system that suggests diseases based on patient symptoms.

An 'Intelligent Technique' where computer systems learn and adapt without following explicit instructions, by using algorithms and statistical models to analyze and draw inferences from patterns in data. Example: A spam filter that learns to identify new types of junk email over time.

A cloud computing model where a vendor provides users access to computing resources such as servers, storage, and networking. The user is responsible for managing the OS, middleware, and applications. Example: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2, where you rent a virtual server.

A cloud computing model where a vendor provides a platform allowing customers to develop, run, and manage applications without the complexity of building and maintaining the infrastructure. The user manages applications and data. Example: Heroku or Google App Engine.

A cloud computing model where a vendor hosts software applications and makes them available to customers over the Internet. The vendor manages everything. Example: Google Docs, Salesforce, or Microsoft Office 365.

An open-source software framework for storing and processing large datasets (Big Data) in a distributed fashion across clusters of inexpensive computers. Example: A company uses Hadoop to analyze terabytes of web server logs to understand user behavior.

A technology that stores data in a computer's main memory (RAM) instead of on disk drives to achieve faster processing and analysis, especially for Big Data. Example: An analytics platform uses in-memory computing to reduce a query that took hours down to seconds.

A new field (either a dimension or measure) that you create in Tableau using a formula or calculation based on existing fields in your data source. Example: Creating a 'Profit Ratio' field by writing the formula `SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales])`.

Semi-structured decisions made by middle management concerning how the organization should achieve the goals set by its strategy. They answer the 'WHAT?' questions. Example: Deciding on the target market for a new product line.

Structured decisions made by operational managers that affect how the firm is run from day to day. They answer the 'HOW?', 'WHEN?', 'WHERE?', and 'WHO?' questions. Example: Deciding on the daily work schedule for customer service representatives.

traps.text: Creating meaningful reports during the 'Transform' step of ETL is WRONG because the Transform step is for cleansing and normalizing data for the warehouse; reporting is a separate BI function that happens after data is loaded.

Believing you can change a project's scope without affecting time or resources is FALSE because the Triple Constraint dictates that changing one variable requires adjusting at least one of the others.
Assuming a keylogger is only software is INCORRECT because it can also be a physical hardware device, like a USB 'Rubber Ducky' that plugs into a computer.
Treating raw data as immediately useful information is WRONG because data are just raw facts; they must be processed and shaped into a meaningful form to become information.
Thinking you own purchased software is FALSE because you only own a license to use it under specific terms, not the software itself.
Considering an IT implementation project to be solely IT's responsibility is WRONG because it requires a holistic approach with management buy-in and user involvement across all affected departments.

Using VLOOKUP in Excel as a full substitute for a relational database is INCORRECT because while it mimics relational lookups, it lacks the data integrity, security, and scalability features of a true DBMS.

Assuming Business Intelligence is only about tools and software is FALSE because its primary purpose is to support timely, data-driven business decisions, which requires managerial involvement and asking the right business questions.
Using OR without parentheses in a SQL WHERE clause that also contains an AND is WRONG because SQL's operator precedence can produce unintended cross-joins, returning far more rows than expected.
Creating a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with excessive, unmanageable detail is WRONG because it obscures the critical path and makes the project harder to track, not easier.

Constantly changing the original business question during analysis is WRONG because while some adjustment is normal, too much change indicates a loss of focus and can derail the entire decision-making process.
Assuming public Wi-Fi hotspots are secure is WRONG because they often have weak security features, making your unencrypted data vulnerable to interception by others on the same network.

Using a Tableau Join when you need a Blend is INCORRECT because Joins combine data row-by-row from tables within the same data source, while Blends combine aggregated data from different data sources.
Failing to normalize database tables is WRONG because it leads to data redundancy and inconsistency, causing data integrity problems when updating or deleting records.
Assuming all project tasks have zero slack time is WRONG because only tasks on the critical path have zero slack; other tasks can be delayed without impacting the project deadline.
Confusing a Data Mart with a Data Warehouse is incorrect because a Data Mart is a smaller, focused subset of a Data Warehouse, typically for a single department or subject area.
Treating a VPN as providing total anonymity is FALSE because while it encrypts your traffic from your ISP, the VPN provider can still see your activity and it doesn't protect against malware.
Believing 'Big Data' is just about volume is incorrect because it's defined by multiple characteristics, often called the 'V's' (Volume, Velocity, Variety), not just size.

Ignoring stakeholder management is a project failure path; assuming the project team and sponsor are the only important parties is WRONG because unidentified stakeholders can introduce unexpected requirements or opposition.
Thinking that a Tableau 'Sheet' and an Excel 'Sheet' are the same is incorrect because in Tableau, a Sheet is a single data visualization (a view), not a grid of cells.

questions.q: What is NOT considered part of an ETL process?
questions.a: Creating meaningful reports.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a primary responsibility of IT project management?
questions.a: Writing the application code for the project.

questions.q: What will a typical LMS (Learning Management System) NOT do?
questions.a: Process university-wide financial payroll.

questions.q: What is cardinality in the context of databases?
questions.a: It measures the number of links in a relationship between data entities (e.g., one-to-one, one-to-many).

questions.q: What is a critical path?
questions.a: The sequence of project tasks that determines the project's total duration.

questions.q: What is the difference between analog and digital?
questions.a: Analog uses continuous physical waves; digital uses discrete binary numbers (0s and 1s).

questions.q: What is a keylogger?
questions.a: A tool that records keystrokes on a computer, which can be software or a physical device like a 'rubber ducky'.

questions.q: What is risk management?
questions.a: The process of identifying, assessing, and developing strategies to mitigate project risks.

questions.q: What is knowledge management?
questions.a: An enterprise-wide effort to collect, store, distribute, and apply digital content and knowledge.

questions.q: What is a conversion rate?
questions.a: The percentage of users who perform a desired action, such as making a purchase on a website.

questions.q: What is a thin client architecture?
questions.a: A client/server model where most processing is done on the server, and the client is mainly for I/O.

questions.q: What is the function of a Primary Key?
questions.a: To uniquely identify each record (row) in a table.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Normalization?
questions.a: To streamline data to minimize redundancy and improve data integrity.

questions.q: What is the primary objective of Business Intelligence?
questions.a: To support timely, data-driven, and objective business decisions.

questions.q: Name the three main types of business analytics.
questions.a: Descriptive, Predictive, and Prescriptive.

questions.q: What are the three components of the Triple Constraint?
questions.a: Scope, Time, and Resources (or Cost).

questions.q: What does DNS stand for and what does it do?
questions.a: Domain Name System. It converts domain names (e.g., google.com) to IP addresses.

questions.q: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS?
questions.a: They are cloud service models that differ in how much of the tech stack the vendor manages vs. the user.

questions.q: What are the four main operations for processing a DBMS?
questions.a: Read, Insert, Modify, Delete data.

questions.q: What is the difference between a data warehouse and a data mart?
questions.a: A warehouse is a large, enterprise-wide data repository. A mart is a smaller subset focused on one subject.

questions.q: What is a 'runaway project'?
questions.a: A project that significantly exceeds its schedule and budget, and fails to perform as specified.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a VPN?
questions.a: To create a secure, encrypted connection over a public network like the internet.

questions.q: In Tableau, what is the difference between a dimension and a measure?
questions.a: Dimensions are categorical fields that set detail level (e.g., 'Region'). Measures are numerical fields that are aggregated (e.g., 'Sales').

questions.q: What are the three key commands in a basic SQL SELECT statement?
questions.a: SELECT (fields), FROM (tables), WHERE (conditions).

questions.q: What is a 'rubber ducky' in the context of IT security?
questions.a: A hardware keylogger, a device that captures keystrokes, often disguised as a USB drive.

questions.q: An exam answer is 'server concentric'. What architectural model is this likely referring to?
questions.a: The Client/Server model, where processing is distributed between clients and a central server.

questions.q: What are the four perspectives of the Balanced Scorecard?
questions.a: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Process, and Learning & Growth.

questions.q: What is the difference between a project and a program in project management?
questions.a: A project has a definite beginning and end to produce a result. A program is an interrelated collection of projects.

questions.q: Name three types of 'Intelligent Techniques' used in Knowledge Management.
questions.a: Any three of: Expert Systems, Machine Learning, Neural Networks, Genetic Algorithms, Fuzzy Logic, Intelligent Agents.

questions.q: In Tableau, what is the difference between a live and an extracted data connection?
questions.a: Live connections query the data source directly; extracts are snapshots for faster performance.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a data dictionary?
questions.a: To store definitions of data elements and their characteristics (metadata).

questions.q: Given the tables on slide 20, what is the result of this query: SELECT PART.Part_Name, SUPPLIER.Supplier_Name FROM PART, SUPPLIER WHERE PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number AND Part_Number = 137;
questions.a: Part_Name: Door latch, Supplier_Name: CBM Inc.

questions.q: What are the three primary actions in a BI analysis process?
questions.a: Acquire Data, Perform Analysis, Publish Results.

questions.q: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
questions.a: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area like an office, while a WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a large geographical area, like a country. The Internet is a WAN.

questions.q: In project management, what is 'earned value' used to measure?
questions.a: It measures completed work to accurately assess the percentage of the project that is complete, comparing it against budget and schedule.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Filled Map and a Symbol Map in Tableau?
questions.a: A Filled Map uses colored geographic areas (like states) to show data. A Symbol Map places symbols of varying size/color at specific geographic points.

questions.q: What is 'Hadoop' used for in a Business Intelligence infrastructure?
questions.a: It enables distributed parallel processing of big data across inexpensive computers.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'ORDER BY' clause in a SQL query?
questions.a: To sort the rows in the result set, either in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.

questions.q: What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile memory? Give an example of each.
questions.a: Volatile (e.g., RAM) loses data when power is off. Non-volatile (e.g., SSD, HDD) retains data without power.

questions.q: What are the three main types of software licenses?
questions.a: Individual, Site License, and Open Source.

questions.q: What is 'in-memory computing' and why is it used for big data?
questions.a: It uses a computer's main memory (RAM) for data storage to avoid slow disk retrieval, drastically speeding up big data analysis.

questions.q: What is the role of a 'user interface' in computer software?
questions.a: It manages the presentation, input, and output between the user and the computer.

questions.q: What are the three levels of management and what type of decisions do they typically make?
questions.a: Upper Mgt: Strategic (unstructured, 'why'). Middle Mgt: Tactical (semi-structured, 'what'). Operational Mgt: Operations (structured, 'how/when/who').
